transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, I came in because people are actually starting to notice how I'm moving lately. It goes back and forth. Sometimes it's like I'm moving underwater... it takes me forever just to answer a question or even get up out of a chair. But then other times, I'm just pacing around my apartment and rubbing my hands together, kind of like I'm trying to shake off a bad call from work. Since other people can actually see me doing this, I figured I should probably get it checked out.

Over the past few weeks or months, have you noticed any significant changes in your mood—like periods where you felt unusually depressed, sad, or down, or conversely, periods where you felt unusually energetic, happy, or irritable?

No, not really. I haven't noticed any big changes in my mood. I mean... I don't think I've been feeling unusually depressed or down, and I definitely haven't had any times where I felt super energetic or unusually happy, either. My mood has felt pretty steady, honestly. It's really just the way I've been moving that's been off.
Are you currently taking any medications, including psychiatric medications, antidepressants, antipsychotics, or any other prescription or over-the-counter drugs?
No, I'm not taking anything. I don't take any prescriptions, and I haven't been taking any over-the-counter stuff either. So, no medications at all right now.
Have you ever been diagnosed with any psychiatric conditions in the past, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, or anxiety disorders?

No, I haven't. I've never actually been diagnosed with any of those... or any psychiatric condition, really. This is honestly my first time getting anything like this checked out, so I don't have any past diagnoses.
Have you ever had a significant head injury, stroke, or any other serious neurological illness or medical condition?
No, nothing like that. I've never had a head injury or a stroke, and I don't have any serious medical conditions that I know of. My physical health has always been pretty normal, honestly.
Does anyone in your family—parents, siblings, grandparents—have a history of movement problems, tremors, or any neurological conditions?
No, not that I know of. I mean, thinking about my parents and grandparents... no, nobody has had any tremors or movement issues. There's no history of any neurological stuff in my family at all.
When did you first notice these movement problems starting? Was it sudden, or did it develop gradually over time?
Well, it's been going on for a while now. I'd say about... maybe 2 years and 3 months? It started right after I was fired from my customer-support job. I guess it kind of just developed after that.
Do you notice that these movement problems—the slowness and the restlessness—get worse or better depending on your stress level or how you're feeling emotionally at the moment?

I haven't really noticed a connection, to be honest. I mean, I guess I'm always kind of stressed or feeling down these days, but the movements just seem to happen no matter what. They don't really get better or worse based on how I'm feeling right then. They're just kind of... always there.
When you notice these movements happening—the slowness or the restlessness and hand rubbing—can you stop them or control them if you try, or do they just happen no matter what you do?

I'm not really sure... I don't think I can control them. They just sort of happen on their own. Like with the hand rubbing, I usually don't even realize I'm doing it half the time, so I can't really stop it. And the slowness, I mean, I can't just force myself to speed up if I try. It all just kind of happens no matter what I do.
If I asked you to sit completely still right now and concentrate very hard on not moving your hands or slowing down your movements, do you think you could do that for, say, 30 seconds or a minute?

I don't think I could, no. Even if I tried really hard to just sit still, it's like... people can actually see me doing it. That's kind of why I came in. People notice that I'm either moving like I'm underwater—taking forever to answer a question or just getting out of a chair—or I'm doing the opposite. Like, I'll be pacing around my apartment and rubbing my hands together like I'm trying to shake off a bad call from work. I can't just turn it off, even for a minute.

You mentioned being fired from your job about 2 years ago. Around that time or shortly after, did you experience any particularly traumatic or emotionally overwhelming event—like a major loss, relationship crisis, or something else very distressing—that seemed connected to when these movements started?

No, not really. I mean, getting fired was definitely stressful, but... there wasn't any other big traumatic event or a relationship crisis or anything like that. It was really just losing the job. I don't remember anything else major happening around then that I could connect to these movements starting.

Throughout the day, are these movements—the slowness and the hand rubbing—happening all the time, or do they come and go? And when you're completely relaxed or distracted, like watching TV or reading, do you still notice them happening?

Well, like I was saying before... it's pretty much all the time. Even when I try to just sit and watch TV or relax, it doesn't really stop. I'll still find myself rubbing my hands together like I'm stressing over a bad call, or if I try to get up from the couch during a commercial, I'm still moving like I'm stuck underwater. 

So, yeah, being distracted doesn't really make it go away. The slowness and the restless feeling... they just kind of stay with me throughout the whole day.
When you're sleeping at night, do these movements—the slowness and the hand rubbing—stop completely, or do they continue even while you're asleep?

I'm pretty sure they stop when I'm asleep. I mean, it's hard to know for sure since I'm out, but no one's ever told me I'm doing it in bed. 

Like I mentioned before, the whole reason I came in is because people can actually see me doing it when I'm awake—either moving like I'm underwater and taking forever to answer or get out of a chair, or the pacing and rubbing my hands like I'm trying to shake off a bad call. But yeah, as far as I know, once I actually get to sleep, all of that finally stops.

When you're doing these movements—like the hand rubbing or the slow movements—does it feel like you're choosing to do them, or does it feel like your body is doing them against your will, almost like something else is controlling your movements?

I don't think it feels like something else is controlling me, no. But I'm definitely not choosing to do it on purpose, either. 

Like I was saying, I really only came in because other people can actually see me doing these things. They'll point out that I'm moving like I'm underwater, taking forever just to answer them or get out of a chair. Or they'll notice me pacing my apartment and rubbing my hands together like I'm trying to shake off a bad call. 

I'm not deciding to do any of that. It's just... my body just sort of does it on its own.

When you're rubbing your hands together or pacing around, do you feel like there's a buildup of tension or an urge inside you that gets relieved when you do these movements, or does it feel more like your body is just moving without any particular urge driving it?

It's more like my body is just moving. I don't really feel this big urge or tension that I need to relieve. 

Honestly, like I keep mentioning, I really only came in because other people can actually see me doing it. They're the ones who notice me pacing my apartment and rubbing my hands together, like I'm trying to shake off a bad call. Or they see the other side of it, where I'm moving like I'm underwater and taking forever just to answer a question or get up out of a chair. 

So, yeah, it's not really about relieving any kind of inner tension for me... it just happens, and it's obvious enough that everyone else sees it.

target_item.manifestation: I came in because people can actually see me either moving like I’m underwater, taking forever to answer or get out of a chair, or else pacing my apartment and rubbing my hands like I’m trying to shake off a bad call.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the subjective experience and volitional control of the psychomotor changes (hand rubbing, slowness) to further characterize this symptom.

patient.answer:
I don't think it feels like something else is controlling me, no. But I'm definitely not choosing to do it on purpose, either. 

Like I was saying, I really only came in because other people can actually see me doing these things. They'll point out that I'm moving like I'm underwater, taking forever just to answer them or get out of a chair. Or they'll notice me pacing my apartment and rubbing my hands together like I'm trying to shake off a bad call. 

I'm not deciding to do any of that. It's just... my body just sort of does it on its own.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the movements are purposeful but irresistible (suggesting conversion disorder/F44.4) versus involuntary neurological movements (suggesting essential tremor or other movement disorder/G25.0). Specifically, assess if the patient experiences an internal urge or tension that is relieved by the movements.
doctor.question: When you're rubbing your hands together or pacing around, do you feel like there's a buildup of tension or an urge inside you that gets relieved when you do these movements, or does it feel more like your body is just moving without any particular urge driving it?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: I came in because people can actually see me either moving like I’m underwater, taking forever to answer or get out of a chair, or else pacing my apartment and rubbing my hands like I’m trying to shake off a bad call.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the internal experience (tension or urge) associated with the pacing and hand rubbing, which are manifestations of the patient's psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
It's more like my body is just moving. I don't really feel this big urge or tension that I need to relieve. 

Honestly, like I keep mentioning, I really only came in because other people can actually see me doing it. They're the ones who notice me pacing my apartment and rubbing my hands together, like I'm trying to shake off a bad call. Or they see the other side of it, where I'm moving like I'm underwater and taking forever just to answer a question or get up out of a chair. 

So, yeah, it's not really about relieving any kind of inner tension for me... it just happens, and it's obvious enough that everyone else sees it.

inference.note: G25.0 (Essential tremor) ruled out. Patient demonstrates involuntary movements without clear neurological basis, onset after psychosocial stressor (job loss), movements are not tremor-like but rather alternating bradykinesia and restlessness/pacing with hand rubbing. No family history of neurological disease, no medication exposure, no structural brain pathology. Movements persist despite distraction, stop during sleep, and patient lacks awareness/control. This pattern is consistent with Conversion Disorder with motor symptoms (F44.4) rather than a primary movement disorder. The temporal relationship to job loss 2+ years ago and the functional nature of the symptoms support conversion disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent abnormal involuntary movements (hand rubbing, pacing, psychomotor retardation) lasting 2+ years following a psychosocial stressor (job loss), without mood changes, medication use, or neurological/medical explanation. The movements are non-volitional but not experienced as externally controlled, occur continuously while awake, cease during sleep, and cause observable functional impact. This clinical presentation is consistent with Conversion Disorder with abnormal involuntary movements (F44.4), where psychological distress manifests as motor symptoms without organic pathology.
